statement: Nine children stand side by side in a line. Each is either a truth-teller, who always tells the truth, or a liar, who always lies. Every child says: "Exactly one of the children next to me is a liar." The two children at the ends each have only one child next to them. How many truth-tellers are in the line?

choices.misconception: I worked out the line correctly but counted the liars instead of the truth-tellers.
I counted only the truth-tellers in the middle of the line and left out the two at the ends.
I guessed the line goes truth-teller, liar, truth-teller, liar, and so on, without checking that a truth-teller in the middle would then have two liars next to him.
I thought they must all tell the truth because they all say the same thing, but then nobody would have a liar next to them.

hints: Is the first child a truth-teller or a liar? What does that force next door?
A liar’s claim is false, so a liar has no liar or two liars beside him. The end child has one neighbour. Try the first child as a liar, then a truth-teller, walking along the line each time.
If the first child is a liar, the line is forced to go L, T, T, L, T, T, L, T, T, and then the last child's claim is false although he is a truth-teller. So the first child tells the truth.

solutions.reliable: Look at the first child, who has only one neighbour. Case 1: the first child is a liar. His claim is false, so child 2 is a truth-teller. Child 2 has exactly one liar beside him and child 1 is that liar, so child 3 tells the truth. Child 3 already has a truth-teller on one side, so child 4 must be the liar. Child 4 lies, and with child 3 telling the truth, child 5 cannot be a liar. Carrying on the same way gives L, T, T, L, T, T, L, T, T. But then child 9 is a truth-teller whose only neighbour, child 8, is not a liar, which contradicts his claim. So Case 1 is impossible. Case 2: the first child tells the truth, so child 2 is a liar. Walking along in the same way gives T, L, T, T, L, T, T, L, T, and child 9 tells the truth with liar child 8 beside him, so everything fits. Every child's statement checks out, and there are 6 truth-tellers. The transferable idea: when each person's type forces the next person's type, try both choices for the first person and follow the chain until it works or breaks.

whyOnTest: Truth-teller puzzles test whether you turn each statement into a firm rule and follow it person by person, rejecting a starting guess the moment it leads to a contradiction.
author: Devansh Sanghavi
